title: Dual Coding
content_html:
Visual learning

Dual Coding

Combine words and visuals — your memory uses both.

What the Research Says

Your brain stores words and images in two separate memory systems, and information is much better remembered when BOTH are used. Dual coding is not the same as “being a visual learner” — learning-styles theory has been debunked. Everyone benefits from combining words with visuals, regardless of any self-reported style preference.

Evidence Base

StudyFindingImpact
Paivio (1971)Original dual-coding theory: verbal and visual memory traces are separate and additive.Two routes to recall is better than one.
Mayer (2001, 2014)Multimedia learning research across 300+ studies: well-designed words+visuals combinations produce ~40% better transfer than words alone.Well-placed visuals turn passive reading into active learning.
Dunlosky et al. (2013)Dual coding is one of the few techniques rated “effective in most contexts” by the Association for Psychological Science.Evidence-backed across age groups and subjects.
Castro-Alonso et al. (2019)Student-generated visuals (drawing) produced bigger gains than pre-made visuals.Draw it yourself, don’t just look at a diagram.

Step-by-Step Method

  1. 1
    Pick a topic with relationships — causes and effects, sequences, comparisons, systems. Dual coding shines when there’s structure to capture.
  2. 2
    Choose the right visual format — annotated floor plan for a Greek temple, labelled sketch of the citadel of Mycenae, comparison table for the three architectural orders, route map for the Odyssey’s geography, flowchart for the journey through the underworld.
  3. 3
    Draw it yourself — by hand or in a simple tool. Don’t just photocopy one from a textbook. The act of creating the visual forces your brain to organise the information.
  4. 4
    Keep text minimal — labels, not sentences. The text and the visual should say different things. Duplicate labels distract (“redundancy effect”).
  5. 5
    Revisit blank versions — redraw your visual with the labels removed. Fill them in from memory. This combines dual coding with retrieval practice.
  6. 6
    Compare versions over time — a week later, redraw from memory. Spot the bits you missed.
Example 1

Draw an annotated floor plan of a typical Greek temple, showing the pronaos (entrance porch), naos (main hall), opisthodomos (rear porch), and the position of the cult statue. Then, in a separate column, sketch the profiles of the three architectural orders — Doric (plain capital, no base), Ionic (scroll volutes, stepped base), Corinthian (acanthus-leaf capital) — and label the key components: column, capital, entablature, frieze, pediment. Mark which order each famous building uses: the Parthenon (Doric), the Erechtheion (Ionic), the Tower of the Winds (Corinthian). A week later, redraw the blank floor plan and order profiles from memory — gaps in the column parts or the plan zones are exactly the details source questions reward.

Example 2

Create a labelled sketch map of the citadel of Mycenae. Mark: the Lion Gate (noting the relieving triangle and heraldic lions), Grave Circle A (shaft graves, gold death masks), the palace complex with its megaron (central hearth, four columns, throne), the cyclopean walls (massive limestone blocks), and the postern gate. Add brief annotations — three words maximum per label — explaining the significance of each feature as evidence of Mycenaean power, religion, or society. Separately, sketch a simple geography map of the Odyssey’s key locations: the Cyclops’s island, Aeaea (Circe), the land of the dead, Scylla and Charybdis, the island of Helios, and finally Ithaca. Connecting the Odyssey map to the Mycenaean sketch reinforces how both texts and artefacts serve as evidence for the Homeric World.

Common Pitfalls

  • Decorative visuals. A picture that looks nice but doesn’t convey information adds cognitive load without the benefit.
  • Copying someone else’s. The learning happens while you make it. A textbook diagram is useful for reference, not for dual coding.
  • Too much text. If your “diagram” is paragraphs joined by arrows, it’s still just text. Keep labels to 2–4 words.
  • Only making it once. One-off diagrams are useful. Ones you redraw from memory over weeks are powerful.

When to Use This

Mid-revision cycle — after you’ve learnt the basic facts and are starting to see connections. Before the exam, try a “one-page summary” for each topic combining a key diagram with 5–10 labelled points. Carry these in your bag. Classical Civilisation is a richly visual subject — artefacts, architectural plans, and temple elevations all appear as sources in the exam. Training yourself to reconstruct these from memory gives you an immediate reference point when a source image appears on the paper.

Quick Reference
~30 minutes per visual

Formats

  2. Architectural orders table
  3. Citadel of Mycenae sketch
  4. Odyssey geography map
